q-80505.name: Question 1
q-80505.problem:
Let $D$ be a finite region enclosed by the curve ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1.$ If 

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y), & (x,y)\in R\cap D \\ 0, & (x,y)\in R∖D\end{aligned}\,\text{and}\,{∬}_{D}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,\text{d}A={∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

which of the following could be the definition of the rectangular domain $R?$

I. $R=[-1,1]\times [-1,1]$

II. $R=[-1,1]\times [0,1]$

III. $R=[-2,2]\times [-2,2]$
q-80505.worked_solution:
First, let's draw our region $D:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14149458/assets/c50e0e01d432b1db736fad09dd5f5b82286e981d88586e848d9b57c8a9910eb0.png)

Notice that if $R$ covers $D$ completely and we define 

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y), & (x,y)\in R\cap D \\ 0, & (x,y)\in R∖D,\end{aligned}
$$

we obtain

$$
{∬}_{D}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,\text{d}A={∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the given rectangles.

- Rectangle II does not cover the region $D.$

- Rectangles I and III covers the region $D$ completely.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

q-86867.name: Question 6
q-86867.problem:
Let $D$ be a finite region enclosed by the curve $\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}=1.$ If 

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{x-y}, & (x,y)\in R\cap D \\ 0, & (x,y)\in R∖D,\end{aligned}
$$

 
which of the following statements are true?

I. ${∬}_{D}{e}^{x-y}\,\text{d}A={∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A,\,$ where $R=[-2,2]\times [-3,3]$

II. ${∬}_{R}{e}^{x-y}\,\text{d}A={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A,\,$ where $R=[-2,2]\times [-3,3]$

III. ${∬}_{D}{e}^{x-y}\,\text{d}A={∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A,\,$ where $R=[-3,3]\times [-2,2]$
q-86867.worked_solution:
First, let's draw our region $D:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14149458/assets/62925844de27c9731b181f17a1bdd912bfa3265176bd62ebda425d182ae8d9e8.png)

Notice that if $R$ covers $D$ completely and we define 

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{x-y}, & (x,y)\in R\cap D \\ 0, & (x,y)\in R∖D,\end{aligned}
$$

we obtain

$$
{∬}_{D}{e}^{x-y}\,\text{d}A={∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the given statements.

- Statement I is false. The rectangle $R$ does not completely cover the region $D.$

- Statement II is false. The rectangle $R$ does not cover the region $D.$ Also, the integrals have not been stated correctly with respect to the domains $R$ and $D$ (they have been swapped).

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the rectangle $R$ covers the region $D$ completely.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

q-80568.name: Question 9
q-80568.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14149458/assets/12acb33aa174f1c174a538a89881dd19245f733c6b39df37f9ebbdc1f86442d5.png)

Consider the region $D$ shown above. If $R=[-3,1]\times [-1,2],$ and

$$
{∬}_{D}({2}^{x}-y)\,\text{d}A={∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

which of the following could be the definition of $f(x,y)?$

I. $\{\begin{aligned}{2}^{x}-y, & (x,y)\in R \\ 0, & (x,y)\notin R\end{aligned}$

II. $\{\begin{aligned}{2}^{x}-y, & (x,y)\in R∖D \\ 0, & (x,y)\in D\end{aligned}$

III. $\{\begin{aligned}{2}^{x}-y, & (x,y)\in R\cap D \\ 0, & (x,y)\in R∖D\end{aligned}$
q-80568.worked_solution:
First, let's draw our region $D$ and rectangle $R:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14149458/assets/56f6557f98674b0f651a781e6226ba9d207273e30136e3396c3aabcf91a64024.png)

Notice that the rectangle $R$ contains the region $D$ completely. 

Now, if we define $f(x,y)$ to be equal ${2}^{x}-y$ on $D$ and to be equal $0$ outside $D,$ we obtain

$$
{∬}_{D}({2}^{x}-y)\,\text{d}A={∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$
